Long-sequence experiments also investigate multiple-edit failures and demonstrate promising improvements with an outer Reed–Solomon code.

The observed improvements may remain valid, but the proposed mechanism needs direct empirical validation or a corrected argument.

The optimality claims substantially exceed the evidence. Matching a redundancy expression over short lengths up to 11 establishes neither finite-length optimality nor asymptotic order-optimality. Decoding is compared only with brute force, omitting natural exact baselines such as enumerating single-edit candidates and using codebook hash lookup. The headline 16.8% cardinality gain corresponds to approximately one percentage point of rate improvement over random selection at length 11.

Guaranteed correction by an exact bounded-distance decoder does not transfer automatically to the proposed embedding-based decoder. Exact reranking cannot recover a correct codeword excluded from the retrieved candidates. Construction over all 4^n candidates, index memory, and actual long-sequence DFS runtimes are not characterized.
